title: Space Force-backed mission does its best impression of Top Gun in orbit
gist: In the Space Force's Victus Haze exercise, Rocket Lab launched its Puma satellite 17 hours after call-up and completed rendezvous and imaging of True Anomaly's Jackal in under 59 hours against an 84-hour requirement, then the two spacecraft ran unscripted pursuit-and-evade maneuvers—the first unclassified demonstration of orbital dogfighting between commercially built satellites.

insights.claim: Rocket Lab rolled its Electron rocket and Puma satellite to the pad and launched on June 19 less than 17 hours after Space Force call-up, against a 24-hour requirement.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Sub-24-hour launch responsiveness is now a demonstrated commercial capability, which is the operational prerequisite for on-demand military space response contracts.
insights.locator: That happened last month, when military officials informed Rocket Lab

insights.claim: Rocket Lab fully activated and prepared Puma for its first orbital maneuver within 38 hours, beating the Space Force's 72-hour requirement, then completed rendezvous and photography in under 59 hours against an 84-hour criterion.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Beating every stated threshold by wide margins is the kind of over-delivery that drives follow-on contract awards—track Rocket Lab's national-security backlog.
insights.locator: Within 38 hours, Rocket Lab had fully activated

insights.claim: Victus Haze builds on Victus Nox, which launched in 2023 with a then-record 27-hour call-up using Firefly Aerospace's Alpha rocket and a Millennium Space Systems satellite, and adds complexity by including a second satellite.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Call-up times fell from 27 to 17 hours in three years—a measurable capability curve for judging the responsive-space program's trajectory.

insights.claim: Rocket Lab ran three independent teams in parallel within the first hour—launch prep, guidance engineers computing a nearly instantaneous launch window to inject Puma near Jackal, and around-the-clock satellite control—and bumped a scheduled commercial launch from the same pad.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Responsive military missions displace commercial manifest slots—a real revenue-timing cost that offsets the headline contract value.
insights.quote: Within that first hour, we basically had three independent teams moving in parallel,
insights.locator: Rocket Lab’s Electron rocket and Puma satellite were in a ready state

themes.theme: Orbital pursuit and evasion demonstrated openly

insights.claim: The exercise demonstrated for the first time in an unclassified setting how future satellites might evade and pursue one another in a conflict, using True Anomaly's Jackal (also called Panther) and Rocket Lab's Puma, built on the Pioneer platform.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Declassifying counterspace maneuver capability is itself a signaling decision—it makes orbital conflict an openly budgeted line item and grows the addressable market.
insights.locator: An ongoing military exercise happening hundreds of miles above Earth

insights.claim: On July 14 the two companies received Mission 2 orders to pursue and evade repeatedly; True Anomaly says Jackal produced a validated mission plan in under 30 minutes from tasking and executed a 23-minute burn sequence to close on Puma.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Sub-30-minute replanning is the tempo metric that separates operationally useful counterspace assets from demonstration hardware.
insights.quote: Jackal’s crew produced a validated mission plan in under 30 minutes from tasking,
insights.locator: The task? Pursue and evade one another over and over again

insights.claim: The exercise ran without coordination between True Anomaly and Rocket Lab and with no scripted target behavior—Puma maneuvered to lose Jackal in ways Jackal's team did not know in advance.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Unscripted adversarial testing is the standard that separates credible military capability from vendor demos—apply the same lens to autonomy claims generally.
insights.quote: It was maneuvering to lose us
insights.locator: All of this was done without coordination

insights.claim: True Anomaly's ground controllers in Colorado managed maneuvers with an algorithm generating hyper-accurate targeting estimates from onboard Jackal measurements.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Onboard-sensing-plus-ground-algorithm targeting is the software layer where defense-space differentiation is accruing, not in the bus hardware.
insights.locator: True Anomaly’s ground controllers, working out of an operations center

insights.claim: Space Systems Command declined to disclose sensor suites, characterization phenomenology, payloads, distances, or docking details, and no photos from the most recent demo have been released.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: The specific redactions—especially docking—hint at capabilities beyond inspection, which is where the program's real strategic value sits.
insights.quote: Due to operational security, further details involving sensor suites for characterization, phenomenology, payloads, distances, or docking will not be shared,
insights.locator: Military and company officials haven’t released any photos

themes.theme: Doctrine and the physics of space dogfighting

insights.claim: The military use case is direct: if an adversary satellite approaches a multibillion-dollar US spy satellite with unknown intentions—something already happening to some degree—forces could launch a shelf-ready satellite into the same orbit to inspect it and perhaps in future take action.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Establishes a standing requirement for stockpiled satellites plus on-call launch—an inventory-carrying business model distinct from traditional space procurement.
insights.locator: It’s easy to see the military utility for this type of capability

insights.claim: True Anomaly CEO Even Rogers, who previously served in a US Air Force space aggressors unit, says orbital dogfighting lacks the drama of aerial combat because the tempo and relative velocities are slower.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Slow relative dynamics mean the competitive edge is in planning software and propellant budget, not reflexes—shapes which suppliers win.
insights.quote: Dogfighting in space doesn’t quite have the drama of an aerial dogfight,
insights.locator: But orbital dogfighting is a lot different

insights.claim: The satellites operate about 300 miles (500 km) up at roughly 17,000 mph, yet their motion relative to each other resembles a choreographed dance rather than a game of chicken.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Corrects the intuitive mental model—orbital engagements are propellant-limited endurance contests, which favors larger delta-v budgets over speed.
insights.locator: It’s important to remember this all played out

insights.claim: The two satellites are designed to swap aggressor and target roles across a series of demonstrations over the next few months, so Victus Haze is an ongoing program rather than a single event.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: A months-long campaign means recurring news flow and repeated performance evidence for both contractors.
insights.locator: There’s more to come on Victus Haze

themes.theme: Surprise as a design feature, and commercial spillover

insights.claim: Rocket Lab knew it would chase a True Anomaly satellite but not which one, because True Anomaly switched from a planned Firefly Aerospace Alpha launch to a SpaceX Falcon 9 rideshare in May—an intentional surprise built into the war game.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Also a quiet data point on launch-provider reliability: a national-security demo moved off Alpha onto Falcon 9.
insights.quote: The idea was it was supposed to be a surprise to exercise the team, and no, we didn’t know what thing we were going to go be chasing,
insights.locator: From Rocket Lab’s perspective, Victus Haze came with an unexpected twist

insights.claim: Rocket Lab's Brian Rogers says a commercial responsive-launch market already exists for customers bumped from rideshares or facing business-critical orbit deadlines, and the company has done three or four such missions in the past year with another likely this year.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Quantifies a real, recurring commercial revenue stream from responsiveness—not just a defense-funded capability.
insights.locator: Most of Rocket Lab’s launches carry commercial satellites

insights.claim: Rogers claims probably only two companies at most in the world can execute a rapid call-up launch, with the commercial version running roughly three months from contract signing to orbit rather than 24 hours.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: A duopoly claim in responsive launch implies pricing power—if true, margin expansion should follow rising national-security demand.
insights.quote: There are just not many companies in the world—in fact, probably only two at most—that you can call and can make that happen,
insights.locator: The 24 hour call-up and RPO mission was very much a national security application

insights.claim: True Anomaly CEO Even Rogers framed the exercise as four years of company effort culminating, with Victus Haze envisioned to remove simulation and learn in the orbital environment against a thinking adversary.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: A 2022-founded startup reaching operational military demonstration in four years shows how fast defense-space entrants can now mature.
insights.quote: Victus Haze was envisioned to remove the simulation and to learn in the orbital environment against a thinking adversary,
insights.locator: There’s more to come on Victus Haze
